title: Solo dev building a live Android idle ARPG with AI: why making the build reject Math.random() saved my codebase
author: YakFederal3939
selftext:
I build Idle Rift RPG solo in about 12 hours a week while keeping it live on Google Play. Using AI coding assistants is the main reason a one-person project can ship features like a 200-floor Boss Labyrinth and cross-device server wallets alongside a day job, yet early on I kept running into a sneaky failure mode: an AI-generated helper would quietly reach for Math.random() or Date.now() inside combat or loot logic.



In an idle RPG where heroes keep hunting for up to 8 hours with the app closed and a server validates runs with the same simulation engine, one hidden non-deterministic call breaks offline progression and causes client and server replays to drift apart. Reviewing every single diff by eye at midnight is not a reliable safety net when you are shipping quickly.



My fix was to separate the game simulation into a pure TypeScript package where time and RNG seeds are explicitly injected, then wire custom lint rules that fail the build the moment anything inside the sim touches global randomness, clocks, or browser globals. Whenever an AI assistant writes or refactors combat math, over 1,700 automated tests run deterministically against fixed seeds before I ever look at an Android bundle.



That shift changed how I prompt and review code completely. Instead of asking an assistant to be extra careful, I ask it to write the test alongside the mechanic and let the linter and test suite catch edge cases on the first pass. The game is free to play on Google Play with optional purchases and optional rewarded ads, and the base pixel art is licensed from Oryx Design Lab and animated procedurally in PixiJS.



For anyone else shipping live games with AI assistance, what automated guardrails or build checks actually caught mistakes before players saw them? If you want to poke at the live Android build while reading, it is on Google Play: [https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.kotmstudios.idleriftrpg&referrer=utm\_source%3Dreddit\_aigamedev%26utm\_medium%3Dpost%26utm\_campaign%3Dai\_determinism](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.kotmstudios.idleriftrpg&referrer=utm_source%3Dreddit_aigamedev%26utm_medium%3Dpost%26utm_campaign%3Dai_determinism)

comments.author: Fancy-Proof-9449
comments.body:
Similar here. My game records your path and replays it against you, so anything nondeterministic shows up fast. The checks that earned their keep:

Map generation runs across 40 seeds in the build and fails if a maze isn't fully connected or if the same seed gives a different map. One mode also plays a whole simulated match and compares a hash of the end state to a stored one, so a change that was meant to be cosmetic can't quietly change gameplay.

The one that reached players before I had a check: purchases. The store code was tested against fake store plugins, but the real error code from Google was being thrown away, so when buys failed I had no idea why. Logging the reason turned out to be a guardrail too.

And +1 on making it write the test with the mechanic. I added one rule on top: a new test doesn't count until I've watched it fail against the old code.
